subUnits.title: 7.1 Les Maladies Courantes
notes: Les Maladies Courantes
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: name common illnesses in French.
Key Concepts:
1. Common Illness Vocabulary:
- MASCULINE: le paludisme (malaria), le choléra (cholera)
- FEMININE: la fièvre jaune (yellow fever), la dysenterie (dysentery), la grippe (flu/influenza)
- The GENDER of each illness noun must be learned with the word — it matters for grammar structures studied next.
2. Why Learning Gender Matters Here:
- When using 'avoir mal à' (studied in Sub-unit B), the contraction depends on the noun's gender.
- Getting article/gender right now prevents errors later.
Formula Box:
Masculine illnesses: le paludisme | le choléra
Feminine illnesses: la fièvre jaune | la dysenterie | la grippe
Analogy:

Learning illness vocabulary is like learning the names of storms before hurricane season: this is not idle academic knowledge, but genuinely USEFUL preparation — being able to correctly NAME 'le paludisme' or 'la grippe' in French is the essential first step toward discussing symptoms, causes, and prevention clearly and confidently.
Common Mistakes to Avoid:
- Learning illness names without their correct article/gender — this will cause errors in the 'avoir mal à' grammar structure studied shortly.
- Confusing 'la dysenterie' (dysentery) with 'la diarrhée' (diarrhoea) — related but distinct medical terms.

quiz.q: What does 'le paludisme' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Le paludisme' means malaria — a masculine noun.

quiz.q: What does 'la fièvre jaune' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'La fièvre jaune' means yellow fever — a feminine noun (fièvre = fever, jaune = yellow).

quiz.q: What does 'la dysenterie' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'La dysenterie' means dysentery — a feminine noun. Do not confuse with 'la diarrhée.'

quiz.q: What does 'le choléra' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Le choléra' means cholera — a masculine noun.

quiz.q: What does 'la grippe' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'La grippe' means flu or influenza — a feminine noun.

quiz.q: What is the grammatical gender of 'le paludisme'?
quiz.explanation: 'Le paludisme' is masculine — 'le' indicates a masculine noun.

quiz.q: What is the grammatical gender of 'la grippe'?
quiz.explanation: 'La grippe' is feminine — 'la' indicates a feminine noun.

quiz.q: Which of these illnesses is masculine?
quiz.explanation: 'Le choléra' is masculine; the others listed here are all feminine.

quiz.q: Why is it important to learn each illness's gender alongside its name?
opts: It matters for grammar structures used later, like 'avoir mal à'
Illness names never require an article
Gender has no practical importance in French
French illness names are always feminine
quiz.explanation: The gender of a noun determines which article contraction to use in structures like 'avoir mal à + body part' studied in the same week.

quiz.q: This week's analogy compares learning illness vocabulary to ___.
opts: learning the names of storms before hurricane season
learning words with no future application
a topic with no real-world usefulness
quiz.explanation: Just as naming storms prepares you for hurricane season, naming illnesses in French prepares you to discuss symptoms, causes, and prevention — practical, real-world knowledge.

subUnits.title: 7.2 Avoir Mal à + Parties du Corps
notes: Avoir Mal à + Parties du Corps
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: use the structure 'avoir mal à' with body parts to describe pain, applying the correct contraction.
Key Concepts:
1. The Structure 'Avoir Mal À':
- To say something HURTS in French: AVOIR MAL À + [body part]
- This uses the verb AVOIR (conjugated) + 'mal' (pain) + 'à' + the body part with its article.
2. OBLIGATORY Contractions of 'À' + Article:
- À + LE → AU (masculine singular): j'ai mal AU bras (my arm hurts)
- À + LA → À LA (no change — feminine singular): j'ai mal À LA tête (I have a headache)
- À + LES → AUX (plural): j'ai mal AUX dents (my teeth hurt)
- À + L' → À L' (no change — before a vowel sound): j'ai mal À L'œil (my eye hurts)
- NOTE: 'à le' and 'à les' NEVER appear in correct French — they MUST contract.
Formula Box:
à + le → AU | à + la → À LA | à + les → AUX | à + l' → À L'
j'ai mal AU bras | j'ai mal À LA tête | j'ai mal AUX dents | j'ai mal À L'œil
Analogy:

The contraction of 'à + le' into 'au' (and 'à + les' into 'aux') is like two words FUSING together when spoken quickly and naturally, the way 'do not' naturally fuses into 'don't' in casual English speech — a permanent grammatical fusion, not just an optional shortcut.
Common Mistakes to Avoid:
- Writing 'à le' or 'à les' — these MUST contract to 'au' and 'aux.' This is NEVER optional.
- Forgetting that 'à la' and 'à l'' do NOT contract — only the masculine singular and plural forms fuse.

quiz.q: What does 'avoir mal à' mean?
opts: To have pain at/in (a body part); it hurts
quiz.explanation: 'Avoir mal à' literally means 'to have pain at' — used to say that a body part hurts.

quiz.q: What does 'à + le' contract into?
quiz.explanation: 'À + le' ALWAYS contracts to 'au' — 'à le' is never used in correct French.

quiz.q: What does 'à + les' contract into?
quiz.explanation: 'À + les' ALWAYS contracts to 'aux' — 'à les' is never used in correct French.

quiz.q: Does 'à + la' contract into a different form?
quiz.explanation: 'À + la' does NOT contract — it stays as 'à la.' Only the masculine singular (à+le) and plural (à+les) contract.

quiz.q: How would you say 'my arm hurts'?
quiz.explanation: 'Le bras' (masculine singular): à + le → au. Correct: 'j'ai mal au bras.'

quiz.q: How would you say 'my teeth hurt'?
quiz.explanation: 'Les dents' (plural): à + les → aux. Correct: 'j'ai mal aux dents.'

quiz.q: How would you say 'I have a headache' (my head hurts)?
quiz.explanation: 'La tête' (feminine singular): à + la → stays à la. Correct: 'j'ai mal à la tête.'

quiz.q: The contraction 'à + le → au' is compared to ___ in this week's analogy.
opts: 'do not' fusing into 'don't' in casual English
a fusion that only happens in writing, never speech
two words that never combine in any language
quiz.explanation: Just as 'do not' fuses into 'don't' in English, 'à le' fuses into 'au' in French — a permanent, obligatory grammatical fusion.

quiz.q: Is 'à le' ever correct in standard French?
opts: No, it must always contract to 'au'
Yes, but only when speaking quickly
Yes, but only in formal writing
Yes, it is always correct as written
quiz.explanation: 'À le' is NEVER correct in standard French — it must always contract to 'au.' This is an absolute rule.

quiz.q: This contraction pattern (à + le/les) appears ___.
opts: only in this one specific health-related context
only in very old, outdated French
throughout French grammar, not limited to talking about pain
quiz.explanation: The contractions au and aux appear throughout French grammar whenever 'à' precedes a masculine or plural definite article — health vocabulary is just a memorable introduction to this rule.
